bio: Jennifer Cabrera-Torres brings nearly two decades of personal injury experience to her role as Managing Partner. She spent more than 15 years as a personal injury paralegal before becoming an attorney, and has always believed in the power of advocacy to change lives.

Born in Atlanta and raised in Gwinnett County by immigrant parents, Jennifer was the first in her family to graduate from college and law school, overcoming the loss of her father days after graduation and becoming a mother during law school. That journey drives her commitment to people who are too often overlooked or underestimated.

Jennifer handles serious injury cases involving car accidents, tractor-trailers, wrongful death and slip-and-fall incidents. She has recovered millions of dollars for her clients and tried multiple cases to verdict. Her litigation experience, combined with personal dedication to each client, makes her a formidable advocate in and out of the courtroom.
Fluent in Spanish, she makes sure every client feels heard, understood and supported throughout the process.

areasFull.name: Motor Vehicle Accidents
areasFull.desc: Crashes are the most common cause of serious injury in Georgia. We investigate fault, deal with the insurers so you don’t have to, and pursue every available policy, including your own underinsured coverage.

areasFull.name: Dog Bites
areasFull.desc: Georgia holds owners responsible when they knew their dog was dangerous or let it run loose in violation of a local leash ordinance. Bites often mean scarring, infection and lasting trauma, especially for children.

areasFull.name: Slip & Fall
areasFull.desc: Property owners must keep their premises reasonably safe. When a wet floor, broken stair or poor lighting causes a fall, the business’s commercial liability insurance is where the claim goes.

areasFull.name: Catastrophic Injury & Wrongful Death
areasFull.desc: When an injury changes a life or ends one, the claim has to account for the whole future: lifetime care, lost income, and the full value of a life.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to hire a personal injury lawyer?
faqs.a: Nothing up front. We work on a contingency fee, which means we are paid a percentage only if we recover money for you. The initial consultation is free.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a claim in Georgia?
faqs.a: Generally two years from the date of injury for most personal injury cases. Exceptions can shorten or extend that deadline, so it is important to call early.

faqs.q: What can I recover through a personal injury claim?
faqs.a: Current and future medical expenses, lost wages, reduced earning capacity, out-of-pocket costs, pain and suffering, and in some cases compensation for scarring or diminished quality of life.
Almost always an insurance company: the at-fault driver’s policy, a business’s commercial liability coverage, or a homeowner’s policy. We examine every available policy, including your own.

faqs.q: Will my case go to court?
faqs.a: The large majority of cases resolve by settlement. We prepare every case as if it will be tried because that produces better offers, and when needed, Jennifer has taken cases to verdict.

faqs.q: What should I do right after an accident?
faqs.a: Get medical care, call the police, photograph the scene and the vehicles, collect witness information, and do not give a recorded statement to the other side’s insurer before speaking with a lawyer.

faqs.q: Should I talk to the other driver’s insurance adjuster?
faqs.a: You are not required to. Adjusters are looking for statements that lower the value of your claim. Let us handle those conversations.

faqs.q: What if I was partly at fault?
faqs.a: Georgia follows modified comparative negligence: you can recover as long as you are less than 50% at fault, and your compensation is reduced by your share of the blame.

faqs.q: What if the at-fault driver has no insurance?
faqs.a: Your own uninsured or underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage may pay your damages. We review every available policy to find coverage.
Yes. Jennifer and our team work in Spanish and English, so you understand every step of your case.

articles.title: What to do in the first 7 days after a crash
articles.excerpt: The steps that protect your health and your claim, and the mistakes insurers are counting on you to make.
body: The first week after a crash shapes much of your claim. Adrenaline hides injuries, insurers call fast, and evidence disappears. Here is what we recommend.

Day 1: get medical care even if you feel fine. Neck, back and head injuries can take days to show up, and an early medical record ties the injury to the crash. Call the police and get the report number.
Days 1 to 3: save photos of the vehicles, the scene and your injuries. Write down witness contact information. Do not post about the accident on social media; insurers look.

Days 3 to 7: the other side’s insurer will probably call asking for a recorded statement. You are not required to give one. Talk to a lawyer first. Keep your medical appointments: gaps in treatment are used to argue your injuries are minor.

articles.title: Georgia’s dog bite law, explained
articles.excerpt: When an owner is liable, how leash ordinances factor in, and what homeowner’s insurance covers.
body: Georgia does not follow a strict-liability rule for dog bites. Under O.C.G.A. §51-2-7, an owner is liable if the dog was dangerous or vicious and the owner carelessly managed it or let it go at liberty.

The second half is the key. A dog running loose in violation of a local leash ordinance is treated as “vicious” under the statute. In most metro Atlanta counties, including Gwinnett, that means an unleashed dog off its owner’s property already meets the test.

Compensation usually comes from the owner’s homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, which typically covers dog bites. Damages include treatment, reconstructive surgery, scarring and emotional trauma, especially for children.
You have two years from the bite to file suit. Photograph the wounds, get the owner’s name, and report the incident to animal control.

articles.title: I fell in a store. Do I have a case?
articles.excerpt: What has to be proven in a premises liability claim and why surveillance video matters so much.
body: Falling in a business does not automatically create a case. Georgia requires proof that the owner had “superior knowledge” of the hazard: they knew or should have known about the wet floor, loose tile or poor lighting, and you did not.

That is why timing matters. If an employee spilled something minutes earlier, the store may not have had a reasonable chance to clean it. If the puddle had been there for hours or was a recurring problem, liability is much clearer.
Surveillance video is often the best evidence, and it is often overwritten within 30 days or less. A lawyer can send a preservation letter immediately so the business must keep it.
Report the fall to the manager before you leave, ask for a copy of the incident report, photograph the area and your footwear, and get medical care the same day.

articles.title: What is my injury case worth?
articles.excerpt: The factors that actually move a claim’s value, and why no one can give you a number on day one.
body: There is no formula. A claim’s value depends on the severity of the injury, the cost of treatment, time missed from work, the effect on your daily life and, decisively, how much insurance coverage exists.

Economic damages are the measurable ones: medical bills, future care, lost wages and reduced earning capacity. Non-economic damages cover pain, suffering and diminished quality of life; a Georgia jury decides those based on its “enlightened conscience.”
Available coverage is often the ceiling. If the at-fault driver carries a $25,000 minimum policy, we look for other sources: your UM/UIM coverage, the driver’s employer, or umbrella policies.
Be wary of anyone who promises a number before your treatment is finished. The real value is known when the prognosis is known.

articles.title: Why truck accident cases are different
articles.excerpt: Federal regulations, multiple liable parties, and evidence that disappears fast.
body: A crash with a tractor-trailer is not just a bigger car wreck. Trucking companies are governed by federal FMCSA regulations on hours of service, maintenance and driver qualification, and every violation can be evidence of negligence.
There are also more potential defendants: the driver, the trucking company, the trailer’s owner, whoever loaded the cargo, and the maintenance shop. Each may carry its own policy.

Key evidence lives on the truck: electronic logging device data, dash cameras and maintenance records. Carriers have rapid-response teams at the scene within hours. An early preservation letter is essential.
We have recovered $1.2 million and $550,000 in Gwinnett County truck cases. Call early; the first days matter.

articles.title: How contingency fees work
articles.excerpt: What “no fee unless we win” actually means, and what to ask before you sign.
body: A contingency fee means the lawyer is paid a percentage of what is recovered, and nothing if there is no recovery. You pay nothing up front, and the initial consultation is free.
The typical percentage in Georgia is one-third if the case settles before a lawsuit is filed, and somewhat more if litigation is required, because the work and risk increase.
Ask about case costs too: medical records, expert witnesses, filing fees. Ask whether they are deducted before or after the percentage, and who bears them if there is no recovery.
A good fee agreement is clear, in writing, and explained to you in your language. If something is unclear, ask before you sign.
